Article
Unsupervised Detection of Pathological Gait Patterns via
Instantaneous Center of Rotation Analysis
Ludwin Molina Arias * and Magdalena Smoleń
Department of Biocybernetics and Biomedical Engineering, Faculty of Electrical Engineering, Automatics,
Computer Science and Biomedical Engineering, AGH University of Krakow, 30 Mickiewicza Avenue,
30-059 Krakow, Poland; msmolen@agh.edu.pl
* Correspondence: arias@agh.edu.pl
Abstract
This study introduces a novel unsupervised framework, ICR-LLS, for detecting pathologi-
cal gait patterns using instantaneous center of rotation (ICR) trajectories of the shank in
the sagittal plane. ICR trajectories were computed from two-dimensional kinematic data
captured at the lateral femoral epicondyle and lateral malleolus for both shanks, producing
four-dimensional multivariate time series for each gait trial. Pairwise trajectory dissimilari-
ties were quantified using circularly aligned Dynamic Time Warping (DTW), preserving
temporal and spatial structure. The resulting dissimilarity matrix was embedded into a
three-dimensional space using a force-directed network layout, enabling intuitive visualiza-
tion of inter-subject gait relationships. Density-based clustering (DBSCAN), enhanced with
a consensus-based ensemble approach, was employed to automatically identify clusters
representing typical (healthy) gait patterns and outliers corresponding to pathological
deviations. The framework is evaluated on a public dataset comprising individuals with
Parkinson’s disease (PD) and healthy controls, achieving a normalized mutual information
(NMI) of 0.449 and a Separation-to-Compactness Ratio (SCR) of 6.754, indicating a mean-
ingful cluster structure. In addition, classification-oriented metrics yield an accuracy of
90%, sensitivity of 70%, and specificity of 96.7%, supporting the method’s effectiveness in
distinguishing pathological gait. By combining minimal 2D kinematic inputs with unsuper-
vised learning, ICR-LLS provides an interpretable framework for the exploratory analysis
of gait variability, and although further validation is required, the findings suggest that
ICR trajectories may serve as a meaningful biomechanical descriptor for characterizing
pathological locomotion.
Keywords: pathological gait; Parkinson’s disease; instantaneous center of rotation; 2D
kinematics; unsupervised clustering; Dynamic Time Warping
1. Introduction
Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a chronic and progressive neurodegenerative disorder that
primarily affects motor function. It is caused by the degeneration of dopaminergic neurons
in the substantia nigra, leading to hallmark motor symptoms such as tremor, rigidity,
bradykinesia, and postural instability. Among these, gait disturbances and impaired
postural control are particularly prominent and often appear early in the disease course,
even before other symptoms become fully evident [1].
To monitor PD progression, clinicians frequently rely on standardized rating scales.
The Hoehn and Yahr scale classifies PD severity into five stages based on motor symptoms
Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 3976 https://doi.org/10.3390/app16083976

--- PAGE 2 ---
Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 3976 2 of 24
and functional independence [2], while the Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale
(UPDRS) provides a more detailed multidimensional assessment, including motor function,
cognitive and emotional changes, activities of daily living, and treatment side effects, with
higher scores indicating more severe impairment [3]. Although these tools are widely used
in clinical settings, they are inherently subjective and may lack the sensitivity to capture
early or subtle motor impairments.
A distinct motor manifestation of PD is the so-called parkinsonian gait, characterized
by a stooped posture, reduced arm swing, stumbling steps, and overall instability [4]. These
gait abnormalities not only reflect the severity of motor dysfunction, but also contribute
significantly to the risk of falls. It is estimated that approximately 70% of PD patients
experience at least one fall annually, and 39% suffer recurrent falls. Importantly, recurrent
falls are associated with a median survival of just six years [5]. Beyond causing physical
injuries such as fractures, falls also lead to fear of falling again, increased caregiver burden,
more frequent hospital visits, and gradual loss of independence.
Given the central role of gait dysfunction in PD, gait analysis has emerged as a valuable
tool for both diagnosis and disease monitoring. By quantifying changes in spatiotemporal
parameters such as stride length, gait speed, and variability, it is possible to detect subtle
motor deficits that may not be apparent during a clinical examination [6]. As a result,
gait analysis is increasingly being used to complement traditional assessment methods,
providing objective information on the functional impact of the disease and supporting the
development of targeted interventions.
Although standard spatiotemporal metrics provide useful information, locomotion
disorders, particularly in neurodegenerative conditions such as PD, often involve a complex
interplay of neurological and musculoskeletal impairments, including involuntary move-
ments, partial paralysis, and balance deficits [7]. These complexities highlight the need
for analytical methods capable of distinguishing pathological gait patterns from normal
ones with greater precision. Traditional approaches often rely on the comparison of key
gait parameters with normative datasets obtained from healthy controls [8]. For basic
measurements such as walking speed or step length, simple numerical comparisons may
be sufficient. However, as the dimensionality and variability of gait data increase, more
advanced analytical tools are required.
To address this challenge, researchers have explored various strategies aimed at
capturing the complexity of gait dynamics. An approach involves the use of geometric
distance-based similarity metrics to analyze multidimensional gait data. For instance,
Lee et al. [9] collected data using sensors placed on the head, waist, and legs as participants
engaged in daily activities such as walking, standing, and climbing stairs. Their method
used these measurements to compute gait similarity and detect deviations from typical
movement patterns. In a related effort, Ramakrishnan et al. [10] proposed a Comprehensive
Gait Asymmetry Metric (CGAM), which applies a modified Mahalanobis distance to
examine gait features derived from both motion capture and force plate data. Their results
demonstrated that CGAM is effective in identifying asymmetries, offering a more sensitive
assessment of gait abnormalities than conventional metrics.
Another widely used strategy involves skeletal modeling, in which simplified repre-
sentations of the human body are created by tracking anatomical landmarks over time [11].
These models allow for the computation of frame-by-frame distance metrics or statistical
descriptors, such as covariance matrices of joint angles, to identify deviations from typical
movement patterns. For instance, Khokhlova et al. proposed a classification framework
based on flexion angles obtained from Kinect data, using the K-nearest neighbors algorithm
to detect abnormalities without requiring prior segmentation of the gait cycle [12].
https://doi.org/10.3390/app16083976

--- PAGE 3 ---
Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 3976 3 of 24
With the increasing availability of high-dimensional gait data, machine learning tech-
niqueshavegainedprominenceintheclassificationofpathologicalmovements. Algorithms
such as neural networks [13], support vector machines [14], and random forests [15] have
achieved a strong performance in distinguishing between healthy and impaired gait, espe-
cially in applications related to PD and post-stroke rehabilitation [16]. These models are
capable of handling both binary classification problems (e.g., healthy versus pathological)
and multiclass problems involving multiple neurological conditions [17]. Beyond classi-
fication, other approaches have focused on modeling the temporal dynamics of gait. For
instance, Chen et al. [18] proposed a method that integrates hidden Markov models with
machine learning techniques to capture and recognize abnormal gait patterns over time,
providing a more nuanced understanding of gait variability in neurological disorders.
While supervised models are powerful, they rely on labeled data and may not gen-
eralize well to new or ambiguous cases. In contrast, unsupervised learning methods can
reveal hidden structures in gait data without the need for predefined categories [19,20]. Sev-
eral studies have applied clustering techniques to characterize gait. Chantraine et al. [21]
employed a dual clustering strategy to capture knee movement trajectories across mul-
tiple planes, allowing for a detailed characterization of joint dynamics. Similarly, Mul-
roy et al. [22] applied non-hierarchical clustering to classify stroke patients based on
spatiotemporal and kinematic gait features observed during the recovery process, revealing
different rehabilitation trajectories between subgroups of patients. These unsupervised
approaches demonstrate the potential of clustering to capture meaningful distinctions in
motor function.
Despite significant advances in gait analysis, some biomechanical parameters remain
insufficiently studied. One of these is the instantaneous center of rotation (ICR), which
defines the point around which a segment rotates at a specific instant in time. The ICR
has been widely used in biomechanical research to study joint stability [23], the relation-
ship between tissue abnormalities and mechanical changes, and lumbar spine mechanics,
particularly in relation to load-dependent variations during lifting tasks [24]. However,
its application to gait analysis, especially for capturing continuous segmental rotations
during locomotion, has been largely neglected. Prior studies have primarily focused on
isolated joint mechanics or specific motor tasks without addressing the dynamic evolution
of the ICR throughout the gait cycle. To our knowledge, no research has yet examined the
trajectories of ICR in the lower extremities as markers of gait dysfunction. This represents
an important gap, as ICR trajectories may offer valuable insights into intersegmental co-
ordination and subtle motor control deficits during walking, which are characteristic of
PD-related gait impairments.
Building on this gap, our previous study [25] introduced ICR trajectories as a mean-
ingful biomechanical descriptor to assess gait dynamics. Motivated by these findings, the
present study proposes an unsupervised framework to detect pathological gait patterns by
analyzing the ICR trajectories of the shank in the sagittal plane. Using pairwise dissimilarity
measures, ICR trajectories are embedded into a 3D space via a self-organizing algorithm,
creating a topological representation of gait similarity. Subsequent cluster analysis uncov-
ers groups of consistent gait patterns and isolates outliers that may potentially indicate
pathological gait. The proposed methodology, named Instantaneous Center of Rotation
of Lower Limb Segments (ICR-LLS), is validated on publicly available kinematic datasets
to distinguish Parkinsonian gait from healthy controls. By leveraging this underutilized
biomechanical descriptor, the proposed ICR-LLS methodology offers a novel, data-driven
framework to improve the detection of subtle motor control impairments in PD through an
unsupervised learning approach without relying on labeled data.
https://doi.org/10.3390/app16083976

2. ICR-LLS Methodology
An overview of the ICR-LLS methodology is presented in Figure 1. The framework
uses ICR trajectories of the shank in the sagittal plane during gait as input data and applies
data-driven techniques to uncover intrinsic gait patterns and group trials with similar
kinematic behavior.

Figure 1. Flow chart of the ICR-LLS methodology illustrating the main processing stages.
The following subsections describe each stage of the framework in detail.
2.1. Computation of Shank ICR Trajectories
During walking, the center of mass (CoM) of the body progresses along the direction
of locomotion, while individual skeletal segments undergo planar motion resulting from
the combined translation and rotation of rigid bodies. For a segment that undergoes planar
motion, its instantaneous kinematic behavior can be fully described by its ICR, defined as
the point in the plane about which the segment is momentarily rotating at a given instant.
To determine the ICR of a body segment, it is necessary to estimate the instantaneous
velocity vectors of two distinct points on the segment. From each point a straight line
perpendicular to its corresponding velocity vector is constructed. These perpendicular
lines originate at the locations of the selected points and represent all possible positions of
the instantaneous center of rotation consistent with the observed motion. The intersection
of the two perpendicular lines uniquely defines the ICR at that instant, as illustrated in
Figure 2.
Shank ICR

Figure 2. Determination of the ICR for the shank segment.

Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 3976 5 of 24
The computational procedure for estimating ICR trajectories follows the methodology
described in our previous work [25]. Building on these findings, the present study focuses
on the shank segment, as its ICR trajectory provides a compact representation of lower-limb
motion that integrates both rotational and translational components of segmental dynamics.
Unlike conventional joint angles or segment orientations, which describe motion at individ-
ual joints, the shank ICR captures relative intersegmental motion, thereby summarizing
coordination patterns across the lower limb.
Using preprocessed gait data, including the positions and velocities of markers placed
at the lateral femoral epicondyle and the lateral malleolus, the ICR trajectories of both
shanks were calculated in the sagittal plane for each gait trial. For a given trial, a multivari-
ate time series was constructed by concatenating the horizontal and vertical components of
the ICR trajectories of the left and right shanks. As a result, each gait trial is represented as
a four-dimensional time-series matrix, capturing the spatiotemporal evolution of shank
rotation throughout the gait cycle.

2.2. Pairwise Comparison of ICR Trajectories
A higher degree of variability between two gait-related time-series is associated with
an increased likelihood that at least one of the corresponding gait patterns exhibits atypical
or pathological characteristics. Consequently, pairwise comparisons between multivariate
ICR trajectories were made in the time domain to quantify gait dissimilarity.
In the proposed pipeline, ICR trajectories are compared without amplitude normaliza-
tion, thereby preserving their original spatial scale. To account for temporal misalignments
arising from stride-to-stride variability, each pair of trajectories is first circularly aligned
using cross-correlation.
Let X = [x1,...,xN] and Y = [y1,...,yN] denote two multivariate ICR trajectories of
equal length N, where each sample xn,yn ∈ R4 represents the horizontal and vertical ICR
components of the left and right shanks at time step n.
The circular cross-correlation RXY(τ) is defined as follows:

Following circular time alignment, trajectory dissimilarity is quantified using Dynamic
Time Warping (DTW), which accommodates non-linear temporal deformations while
preserving the spatial structure of the trajectories.

2.3. Embedding of ICR Trajectories in a Low-Dimensional Space
The gait data were modeled as a fully connected weighted network, where each
node represents an individual gait trial, and edge weights encode pairwise DTW-based
dissimilarities. To obtain an interpretable low-dimensional representation, a force-directed
layout algorithm was employed to embed the data in a Euclidean space [26].
Within this framework, nodes are treated as physical particles subjected to repulsive
and attractive forces, both defined as functions of pairwise dissimilarity dij between gait
trials i and j and their current spatial positions x(i) and x(j).
The magnitude of the repulsive force between nodes i and j is defined as:
fr(i, j) =
CK2
∥x(i) − x(j)∥
eαdij (7)
while the magnitude of the attractive force is given by:
fa(i, j) =
∥x(i) − x(j)∥2
K
e
γ
dij (8)
where C controls the strength of repulsion, K denotes the natural spring length, and α and
γ are tuning parameters that regulate the influence of dissimilarity. Both forces act along
the unit vector connecting nodes i and j, ensuring that the interactions are directionally
consistent in the embedding space.
https://doi.org/10.3390/app16083976

--- PAGE 7 ---
Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 3976 7 of 24
Due to the fully connected nature of the network, every pair of nodes simultaneously
experiences both attractive and repulsive interactions. Through iterative position updates,
the system evolves toward a configuration that minimizes the overall potential energy,
computed as the sum of squared forces acting on all nodes.
The resulting embedding preserves the relational structure encoded in the dissimilar-
ity matrix: gait trials exhibiting higher similarity are positioned closer together, whereas
more dissimilar trials are spatially separated. This low-dimensional representation, there-
fore, provides an intuitive and unsupervised visualization of the relationships among
gait patterns.
2.4. Cluster Analysis
To identify latent structures within the low-dimensional representation of the gait-
related data, Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN)
is applied to the resulting embedding. DBSCAN detects dense regions of points while
explicitly modeling noise, making it well suited to identify atypical gait patterns without
requiring a predefined number of clusters [27].
Within this framework, the clustering procedure is designed to identify a compact
reference group representing typical (healthy) gait patterns, while trials that exhibit patho-
logical or atypical gait are treated as outliers. These outliers capture deviations from
normative behavior rather than forming a uniform pathological category, reflecting the
inherent heterogeneity of gait disorders.
Cluster performance was quantitatively evaluated using Normalized Mutual Informa-
tion (NMI), which measures the agreement between cluster assignments L = {l1,...,lN}
and known clinical labels G = {g1,..., gN}, and is given by:
NMI(L,G) =
2 MI(L,G)
H(L) + H(G)
(9)
where MI(L,G) denotes mutual information and H(·) denotes Shannon entropy. The NMI
values range from 0, indicating that there is no correspondence, to 1, representing perfect
alignment with the truth of the ground.
In addition to evaluating agreement with external labels, the internal structure of
the clusters was examined using the Separation-to-Compactness Ratio (SCR). This metric
captures both the cohesion of individual clusters and the distinction between different
clusters. Specifically, the compactness of a cluster Ck is defined as the average distance of its
members to the centroid of the cluster, while the separation between clusters is quantified
as the minimum Euclidean distance between the centroids of all pairs of clusters:
Compactnessk =
1
|Ck| ∑
xi∈Ck
∥xi − µk∥2
(10)
Separationk =
1
|O| ∑
xj∈O
∥xj − µk∥2
(11)
where xi represents a data point within the cluster Ck, xj represents a data point in the set
of outliers O, µk is the centroid of the cluster Ck, |Ck| denotes the number of points in that
cluster and |O| denotes the number of outliers.
The SCR is then expressed as:
SCR =

Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 3976 8 of 24
High SCR values indicate compact and well separated clusters, providing a label-
independent assessment of cluster quality.
It is important to note that, in this study, DBSCAN is formulated as an anomaly
detection approach in which healthy controls form a unique dominant cluster (k = 1)
and pathological cases are primarily identified as outliers. Within this framework, SCR
quantifies the separation between outliers and healthy clusters in relation to their internal
compactness, providing a meaningful indicator of abnormality despite the presence of
noise points.
3. Case Study
3.1. Dataset
To evaluate the proposed framework, two publicly available gait datasets were em-
ployed. This section describes the original characteristics of the datasets as provided by
their respective authors; the specific selection of participants and the variables used in this
study are detailed in the subsequent subsection.
The first dataset [28] was obtained from the Laboratory of Biomechanics and Motor
Control at the Federal University of ABC (Brazil) and includes gait recordings from 26 in-
dividuals diagnosed with PD, with a mean age of 66.3 years. During data acquisition,
participants walked on a 20-m walkway at a comfortable, self-selected speed while motion
was captured using a 12-camera Raptor-4 system (Motion Analysis Corp., Rohnert Park,
CA, USA) operating at 150 Hz. A total of 44 reflective markers were placed according to the
recommendations of the International Society of Biomechanics (ISB), including 26 markers
on the lower limbs and 18 on the upper body. Each participant performed 20 walking
trials across two sessions: one in the dopaminergic ON state and one after at least 12 h of
withdrawal from medication (OFF state).
The second dataset [29] was provided by the Multidisciplinary Motor Center Antwerp
(MMCA) and includes gait recordings from a heterogeneous cohort of 138 neurologically
intact individuals (aged 21 to 86 years) and 50 individuals post-stroke (aged 19 to 85 years).
Motion capture was performed using an 8-camera Vicon T10 (Vicon Motion Systems Ltd,
Oxford, UK) system operating at 100 Hz.
3.2. Data Processing
To allow a comparative analysis between groups, data from 30 neurologically intact
healthy participants and 10 individuals diagnosed with PD in the OFF medication state
were selected from the original datasets. The primary inclusion criterion was to ensure
comparable demographic distributions between groups, particularly in terms of age, to
minimize possible confounding effects. The healthy group spans an age range of 52 to
86 years, while the PD group spans 44 to 81 years, with substantial overlap between
distributions. Sex was not used as a stratification variable.
From the MMCA dataset, only neurologically intact participants were retained, while
all post-stroke individuals were excluded from further analysis.
Table 1 summarizes the demographic and anthropometric characteristics of all par-
ticipants included in the study, including age, gender, body mass, height, and body mass
index (BMI), as well as their corresponding clinical state (Healthy or PD).
Raw motion capture data, stored in C3D format, were imported into the open-source
software Mokka 0.6.2 (INRIA, France) for initial visualization and quality inspection. The
Sagittal-plane coordinates of the anatomical markers were subsequently exported and
processed in MATLAB R2025b (MathWorks, Natick, MA, USA). Figure 3 shows the set of
markers included in the selected datasets.

Two anatomical landmarks, the lateral femoral epicondyle and the lateral malleolus,
were selected bilaterally due to their consistent presence across biomechanical models in
both datasets. Gait cycles were segmented using the vertical displacement of the hip marker
as a reference. Each gait cycle exhibits three local minima in the vertical hip trajectory
corresponding to key events of the stride. These minima were automatically detected by
analyzing the slope of the trajectory, allowing for precise identification of the boundaries
of the gait cycle. Then each segmented cycle was interpolated to 200 samples to ensure
temporal consistency between cycles. Within each cycle, marker trajectories were averaged
to obtain representative motion patterns. The numerical differentiation of these averaged
trajectories yielded marker velocities, which were subsequently smoothed using a moving
average filter over three samples and then used to compute the ICR trajectories of the shank
following the procedure described in Section 2.1.
https://doi.org/10.3390/app16083976

Figure 3. Processing of the kinematic data contained in the selected data sets using Mokka. (a) Iso-
metric view. (b) Sagittal Plane.
To remove the dependence of the ICR trajectories on the global reference frame used
during the gait trials, the ICR trajectories were expressed relative to the center of mass of
the body (COM), producing normalized trajectories defined as follows:
ICRN = ICR − COM (13)
In this representation, values close to zero indicate that the instantaneous center of
rotation is located near the COM.

Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 3976 11 of 24
Vertical ICR values reach substantially larger magnitudes than horizontal values,
particularly in subjects with PD. In these participants, several peaks exceed the range
displayed, reflecting higher amplitudes compared to healthy controls. Additionally, in both
groups, there are portions of the gait cycle in which the ICR approaches zero, indicating
that it is located near the center of mass of the body.
Although the overall trajectory patterns are broadly similar between the groups, PD
subjects exhibit more pronounced asymptotic patterns and greater variability, especially
along the vertical axis. These observations suggest a reduced rotational excursion of the
shank in PD, reflecting a more rigid lower-limb movement compared to healthy controls.
3.3.2. Dissimilarity Matrix
Figure 5 shows the dissimilarity matrix computed from pairwise comparisons of the ICR
trajectories of the shank for individuals with and without PD using DTW-based dissimilarity.
Gait Trials

Figure5. DissimilaritymatrixofshankICRtrajectoriescomputedusingDTW-basedpairwisecomparisons.
The matrix reveals patterns that partially support the initial hypothesis of the study.
Comparisons among healthy controls, located in the upper-left corner, are predominantly
of a cool color, indicating a high similarity in gait patterns. Comparisons between healthy
controls and PD patients, represented in off-diagonal blocks (lower-left and upper-right
corners), show warmer colors, reflecting greater divergence between the two groups. In
particular, comparisons among PD patients, in the lower-right corner, exhibit the warmest
colors, indicating substantial variability within this group despite a common diagnosis.
This suggests that while some PD patients show gait patterns similar to healthy controls,
others show pronounced deviations, highlighting the presence of outliers and heterogeneity
in pathological gait.
3.3.3. Self-Organized Network
The DTW-based dissimilarity matrix was employed to construct a force-directed
self-organizing network in which each node represents an individual gait trial. The net-
work embedding was generated using MATLAB’s built-in force-directed layout algorithm,
which determines node positions through an iterative force-relaxation process. This im-
plementation follows the general force-directed principles outlined in the previous section
https://doi.org/10.3390/app16083976

--- PAGE 12 ---
Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 3976 12 of 24
while internally handling model parameters and numerical settings within the optimized
computational framework of MATLAB.
Two network representations were obtained: a two-dimensional layout and a three-
dimensional layout, as illustrated in Figure 6. In both cases, node positions were computed
through an iterative simulation consisting of 3,000,000 iterations, providing a stable and
well-structured spatial organization of the network.
Figure 6. Self-organized network representation of gait trials. (a) Two-dimensional embedding.
(b) Three-dimensional embedding.
Both embeddings demonstrate a clear separation between the groups. In the two-
dimensional layout, nodes corresponding to healthy gait trials form a compact cluster,
reflecting low intra-group variability. Gait trials performed by individual with PD are
usually located outside of this central cluster and often appear as outliers; although some
form smaller subgroups, indicating partial similarity between certain patients.
Given the pronounced differentiation evident in the two-dimensional embedding and
the compactness of the healthy cluster, subsequent analyzes focus on the two-dimensional
layout, which offers a simpler and equally informative representation of the relationships
between gait trials.
3.3.4. Clustering
To automate the detection of natural groupings in gait data, we applied density-based
clustering using the DBSCAN algorithm on the DTW-derived graph.
A systematic grid search was performed to explore the effects of two DBSCAN hyper-
parameters: the neighborhood radius (ε) and the minimum number of points per cluster
(MinPts). Each configuration was evaluated using NMI and SCR, excluding trivial solutions
that consist of a single cluster with no separation. Figure 7 shows the resulting performance
grid and reveals a clear inverse relationship between NMI and SCR: parameter settings
that maximize agreement with the ground truth do not necessarily yield the most compact
and well-separated clusters.
This inverse trend suggests that clusters with higher internal cohesion and separation
may not recognize all individuals from the same clinical group, particularly in heteroge-
neous PD samples. Based on the grid search, we identified configurations that maximized
NMI and SCR separately, serving as representatives for further cluster inspection.

To improve cluster robustness and mitigate hyperparameter sensitivity, we applied a
consensus-based ensemble approach. DBSCAN was repeatedly applied across the hyper-
parameter grid and a co-association matrix was computed, indicating the fraction of runs
in which each pair of subjects was assigned to the same cluster. Hierarchical agglomerative
clustering was then applied to the co-association matrix to derive the final consensus
clustering. Figure 10 shows the resulting co-association matrix.

3.4. Performance Evaluation of the ICR-LLS Methodology
To assess the performance of the proposed ICR-LLS methodology, a benchmarking
strategy was adopted. Since most existing studies on Parkinsonian gait analysis rely on
supervised classification models trained on labeled data, a direct comparison with the
proposed unsupervised framework is not straightforward. To address this, two complemen-
tary evaluation approaches were considered. First, the clustering results were evaluated
using standard classification metrics, allowing comparison with supervised methods re-
ported in the literature. Second, to provide a more direct and methodologically consistent
comparison, a baseline analysis was conducted on the same dataset using conventional
gait features within the same clustering framework.
3.4.1. Benchmark Against Supervised Learning Methods Reported in the Literature
For the purpose of comparison with supervised learning approaches, clustering out-
comes are mapped to clinical labels and evaluated using standard classification metrics.
Within this framework, pathological subjects are treated as anomalies (outliers), while
healthy controls define the reference group (normal). Consequently, true positives corre-
spond to pathological subjects correctly identified as outliers, true negatives to healthy
controls correctly assigned to the main cluster, false positives to healthy controls incorrectly
labeled as pathological, and false negatives to pathological subjects that remain within the
healthy cluster.
Confusion matrices are computed for the three analyzed configurations: (i) maximum
NMI, (ii) maximum SCR, and (iii) consensus solution. Figure 12 presents the correspond-
ing results.

Case NMI SCR Sn (%) Sp (%) Acc (%) Precision (%) F1-Score
Max NMI 0.451 6.229 80.00 93.33 90.00 80.00 80.00
Max SCR 0.220 9.654 20.00 100.00 80.00 100.00 33.33
Consensus 0.449 6.754 70.00 96.70 90.00 87.50 77.80
Maximizing NMI yields the highest agreement with clinical labels, resulting in bal-
anced performance with high accuracy (90%) and sensitivity (80%) and good specificity
(93.3%). However, this configuration does not explicitly prioritize separation between the
main cluster and outliers.
In contrast, maximization of SCR promotes highly compact and well-separated struc-
tures, but at the expense of detection performance, as reflected by very low sensitivity
(20%) and reduced accuracy (80%). Although specificity and precision reach their maxi-
mum values (100% and 100%, respectively), the low F1-score (33.3%) indicates a strong
bias towards correctly identifying the majority (healthy) class while failing to detect most
pathological cases.
The consensus configuration provides the best trade-off between both criteria. It
achieves strong agreement with clinical labels (NMI = 0.449) while preserving structural
organization (SCR = 6.754). This results in robust overall performance, with high accu-
racy (90%), good sensitivity (70%), high specificity (96.7%) and the best balance between
precision (87.5%) and F1-score (77.8%).

Compared to previous studies, higher performance values are generally reported, par-
ticularly in terms of accuracy and sensitivity, with many methods exceeding 95%. However,
these approaches are predominantly based on supervised learning and rely on ground
reaction forces or three dimensional kinematic data, whereas the proposed methodology
operates using a reduced set of kinematic inputs within an unsupervised framework.

3.4.2. Benchmark Against Conventional Gait Feature Representations
For a fair comparison, the same dataset was analyzed using a conventional gait repre-
sentation based on joint kinematics. Instead of ICR trajectories, knee joint flexion/extension
angles from both lower extremities were considered, as they provide a representative
description of the gait dynamics of the sagittal-plane, analogous to the ICR representation
based on the shank.
From these signals, conventional spatiotemporal and kinematic features were ex-
tracted, including maximum knee flexion, range of motion (ROM), cadence of both lower
limbs. Subsequently, the same clustering framework was applied using DBSCAN. As in
the proposed methodology, a grid search was performed on the DBSCAN parameters, eval-
uating both NMI and SCR to identify optimal configurations, and a consensus strategy was
employed to obtain a robust solution. The grid search identified ε = 3.4 with MinPts = 3 as
the optimal configuration to maximize NMI, while the optimal configuration of SCR was
obtained at ε = 0.85 with MinPts = 3.
Figure 13 shows the clustering structure obtained in the PCA-reduced feature space.
Although a degree of class separability can be observed between healthy controls and PD
subjects, the resulting configuration exhibits a markedly weaker discriminative structure
compared to the proposed representation. Notably, a non-negligible number of PD subjects
are embedded within the region primarily associated with the healthy cluster, which signif-
icantly complicates their identification as outliers. Furthermore, the cluster corresponding
to healthy controls does not display a well-defined compact geometry; instead, it suggests
the presence of intra-cluster heterogeneity, as evidenced by the emergence of two partially
separable subregions within the same cluster.

proposed ICR-LLS methodology and the conventional baseline based on gait features
in all the evaluated configurations. Since both methods are unsupervised, a direct com-
parison using clustering validity metrics is possible. In addition, classification-oriented
performance measures have been reported to provide a more comprehensive evaluation
of the ability of each approach to separate healthy and pathological gait patterns in an
anomaly-detection setting.

ICR-LLS Methodology Conventional Gait Feature-Based Approach
Max NMI Max SCR Consensus Max NMI Max SCR Consensus
NMI 0.451 0.220 0.449 0.367 0.004 0.101

The baseline based on conventional gait features consistently underperforms the pro-
posed ICR-LLS approach in all configurations. The Max NMI solution achieves moderate
agreement with clinical labels (NMI = 0.367) and high specificity (100.0%), but limited
sensitivity (40.0%), indicating a bias toward correctly identifying healthy controls while not
detecting a substantial portion of pathological cases. In contrast, the Max SCR configuration
prioritizes structural separation (SCR = 9.100) at the expense of clinical relevance, resulting
in very low specificity (6.7%) and accuracy (27.5%), as well as a reduced F1-score (38.3%),
suggesting an unstable and clinically non-interpretable clustering solution. The consensus
configuration provides a more balanced behavior, improving overall robustness (77.5%)
and specificity (90.0%), but still exhibits limited sensitivity (40.0%) and a lower F1-score
(47.1%) compared to the ICR-LLS method.
These results indicate that, under the same clustering framework, the baseline using
conventional gait features yields weaker separability and reduced robustness, while the
proposed ICR-LLS representation consistently provides a more balanced detection of
pathological patterns and a more stable healthy cluster structure.
4. Discussion
The results of this study demonstrate that the ICR-LLS methodology effectively cap-
tures clinically relevant differences in gait patterns between individuals with PD and
healthy controls, providing both quantitative and qualitative insight into locomotor alter-
ations. Analysis of ICR trajectories (Figure 4) revealed that PD subjects exhibit increased
vertical displacement amplitudes, asymmetrical trajectories and, in some cases, asymptotic
trajectory shapes, as well as irregular phase timing. The presence of asymptotic behavior is
particularly meaningful from a biomechanical perspective, as it arises when the segment
undergoes predominantly translational motion with a reduced rotational component. This
condition is consistent with increased joint stiffness, particularly in the knee, where limited
flexion and extension reduce rotational excursion and cause the shank to behave more as a
rigid segment. These features are consistent with well-documented motor impairments
in PD, including rigidity, bradykinesia, and impaired intersegmental coordination. Since
the ICR reflects both rotational and translational components of segment motion, these
alterations indicate a change in coordinated lower-limb mechanics rather than isolated
joint abnormalities.
In contrast, healthy controls exhibit smoother, more periodic, and spatially consistent
trajectories with lower intragroup variability, reflecting stable intersegmental coordination
and efficient biomechanical control. This contrast highlights the ability of ICR trajectories
to encode underlying biomechanical constraints and neuromuscular control strategies
associated with both normal and pathological gait.
These observations are further supported by the DTW-based dissimilarity matrix
(Figure 5), where healthy controls consistently present low pairwise dissimilarities, indi-
cating homogeneous gait patterns. In contrast, PD participants exhibit higher intra-group
https://doi.org/10.3390/app16083976

--- PAGE 19 ---
Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 3976 19 of 24
variability, reflecting the heterogeneous manifestation of the disease. In particular, some
individuals show gait patterns close to normality, while others show pronounced devia-
tions, suggesting that PD-related gait impairment exists along a continuum rather than as a
strictly binary condition.
Theself-organizedlow-dimensionalnetworklayoutprovidesanintuitivevisualization
of these differences (Figure 6). Healthy controls form a compact cluster, reflecting highly
uniform gait patterns, while PD subjects are more dispersed, forming small subgroups or
appearing as outliers. This dispersion highlights the ability of ICR-LLS to detect gait devia-
tions and to identify subpopulations of PD patients whose gait remains partially preserved.
Such granularity is difficult to achieve with conventional binary classification approaches
and supports the use of unsupervised representations for exploratory gait analysis.
Clustering analyzes using DBSCAN highlight an inherent trade-off between intrinsic
cluster structure and external agreement with clinical labels. From a methodological perspec-
tive, optimizing for NMI favors solutions that align with known diagnostic categories, which
in this controlled setting results in a dominant healthy cluster and subjects with PD primarily
identified as outliers. However, in unsupervised clinical scenarios, where ground-truth labels
areunavailable, thevalidityoftheclustermustbebasedoninternalstructure-basedcriteria. In
this context, metrics such as the SCR provide a more appropriate assessment of cluster quality,
as they quantify cohesion and separation independently of clinical annotations. Nevertheless,
maximizing SCR alone may bias the solution toward globally compact structures, potentially
reducing sensitivity to subtle or early-stage gait abnormalities by favoring homogeneous
cluster formation over the detection of rare deviations.
This trade-off between structural compactness and sensitivity to atypical patterns mo-
tivates the use of a consensus-based clustering strategy. By aggregating multiple DBSCAN
solutions across parameter settings, the proposed approach mitigates hyperparameter sen-
sitivity and stabilizes cluster assignments. Importantly, this ensemble formulation allows
the method to maintain robustness in identifying consistent patterns of gait deviation while
maintaining sensitivity to heterogeneous pathological manifestations, which is essential in
unsupervised clinical analysis where disease boundaries are not explicitly defined.
To contextualize these findings, Table 5 summarizes clinical scores (UPDRS-II, UPDRS-II
walking subscore, UPDRS-III, UPDRS-III walking subscore and Hoehn & Yahr stage) for sub-
jects with PD during OFF-state walking trials, along with their ICR-LLS classification results.
Table 5. Clinical characteristics of subjects with medically diagnosed PD in the OFF medication state
and corresponding classification outcomes obtained using the ICR-LLS methodology.
Subject UPDRS-II UPDRS-II (Walking) UPDRS-III UPDRS-III (Walking) H&Y ICR-LLS Diagnosis
31 13 2 27 2 3 Healthy
32 11 3 16 2 2 PD

Analysis of Table 5 indicates that inconsistencies between clinical diagnosis and ICR-
LLS assignments are predominantly observed in participants with mild gait impairments.
Specifically, subjects 31, 33, and 39 were assigned to the healthy cluster despite a clinical
diagnosis of PD. These individuals exhibit relatively low UPDRS-II and UPDRS-III walking
https://doi.org/10.3390/app16083976

--- PAGE 20 ---
Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 3976 20 of 24
subscores (1–2), indicating subtle gait alterations. Their Hoehn & Yahr stages (2–3) cor-
respond to mild-to-moderate disease severity, suggesting that their kinematic deviations
during OFF-state walking were not sufficiently pronounced to be detected as pathological
by the ICR-LLS framework. In contrast, subjects correctly classified as PD, including 32,
34, 35, 36, 37, 38, and 40, showed more pronounced gait deviations that were effectively
captured by the ICR-LLS methodology.
To assess whether the structures identified from the ICR trajectories during gait exhibit
statistically significant differences in clinical variables, we employed the Mann–Whitney
U test, a non-parametric method suitable for comparing two independent groups when
normality cannot be assumed. Although the ICR-LLS framework inherently produces
a dominant cluster (corresponding to healthy controls) and a set of outliers (primarily
associated with PD), for statistical analysis these subsets are interpreted as two distinct
groups. This allows a review of whether the distributions of clinical variables differ
significantly between the normative cluster and the anomalous population detected.
The analysis did not reveal significant differences between the groups for age
(p = 0.0558) and BMI (p = 0.1010), indicating that the separation is not driven by de-
mographic factors. In contrast, statistically significant differences were observed for clinical
measures associated with motor impairment in PD, including UPDRS-II (p < 0.001),
UPDRS-III (p < 0.001), UPDRS-II walking (p = 0.0001), UPDRS-III walking (p = 0.0015)
and Hoehn & Yahr stage (p < 0.001).
These findings demonstrate that, although derived from an unsupervised anomaly
detection framework, the partition induced by ICR-based clustering aligns with clinically
significant differences in the severity of motor symptoms. In this sense, the combination
of a dominant cluster and outliers can be interpreted as an implicit separation between
normative and pathological gait patterns.
Most previous studies (Table 3) report very high accuracy, sensitivity, and speci-
ficity, often exceeding 95%, particularly those relying on ground reaction forces or three-
dimensional kinematics. These results reflect the strong discriminative power of high-
dimensional biomechanical features combined with supervised learning frameworks opti-
mized for classification. By contrast, the ICR-LLS methodology adopts a fundamentally
different approach. Rather than relying on GRFs or high-dimensional 3D kinematics, it
analyzes two-dimensional shank ICR trajectories using unsupervised, data-driven methods.
Despite reduced data dimensionality and the absence of supervised training, the method
achieves high specificity (96.7%) and a competitive F1-score (77.8%), indicating a strong
ability to correctly identify healthy controls while maintaining a balanced trade-off between
precision and recall in detecting pathological gait patterns associated with PD.
The moderate sensitivity (70%) reflects the intrinsic trade-off of the proposed anomaly-
detection framework. In contrast to supervised classifiers that often maximize overall
accuracy, ICR-LLS prioritizes the reliable identification of the normative (healthy) gait
pattern, which results in fewer false positives but a higher number of false negatives.
Analysis of misclassified participants reveals that these individuals exhibit only subtle
gait deviations in clinical assessments, placing them near the boundary between normal
and pathological locomotion. This suggests that the method is conservative in labeling
pathological cases, focusing on clear deviations from typical gait behavior.
A direct comparison with a conventional gait feature-based baseline further highlights
the contribution of the proposed representation. By applying the same clustering frame-
work (DBSCAN algorithm) to standard sagittal-plane features, the resulting clusters can be
directly contrasted with those derived from ICR trajectories, allowing a rigorous assessment
of their relative ability to discriminate between PD and healthy controls. As presented in
Table 4, the conventional gait feature-based approach consistently underperformed the
https://doi.org/10.3390/app16083976

--- PAGE 21 ---
Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 3976 21 of 24
ICR-LLS method, exhibiting weaker separability. This is also illustrated in Figure 13, where
several gait trials from individuals with PD appear highly intermingled with the control
group, making them difficult to separate using clustering methods.
From a practical perspective, ICR-LLS offers important advantages in terms of applica-
bility and interpretability. Unlike GRF-based methods that require force plates or 3D motion
capture systems, the proposed framework relies on a limited number of sagittal-plane land-
marks, allowing compatibility with simplified acquisition systems such as monocular
video setups. This facilitates deployment in clinical and outpatient settings and supports
longitudinal monitoring. Additionally, the self-organized network representation provides
an intuitive visualization of gait variability, capturing the heterogeneity inherent in PD
without imposing rigid class boundaries.
Nevertheless, several limitations should be acknowledged. The exclusive focus on
2D shank kinematics may not fully capture multi-planar or compensatory movements,
potentially limiting sensitivity for certain gait phenotypes. In addition, current validation
is restricted to a controlled scenario involving healthy controls and individuals with PD.
Extending the framework to other neurological conditions, such as stroke or multiple
sclerosis, introduces additional complexity, as these populations exhibit high intra-class
variability and may not conform to a single-cluster-plus-outliers structure. Therefore,
generalization to multi-pathology scenarios remains an open challenge and an important
direction for future research.
Future work will focus on integrating additional biomechanical features, extending
the framework to larger and more heterogeneous datasets, and exploring longitudinal
analyzes to support early detection and personalized disease monitoring.
5. Conclusions
This study introduced and evaluated a novel unsupervised learning framework, ICR-
LLS, designed to detect pathological gait patterns using instantaneous center of rotation
trajectories derived from minimal two-dimensional kinematic data. The central aim was to
determine whether subtle and overt gait deviations could be captured without relying on
high-dimensional signals such as ground reaction forces or full 3D motion capture. To this
end, the proposed methodology integrates four sequential components: computation of
shank ICR trajectories, pairwise comparison through DTW-based dissimilarity measures,
embedding of inter-subject relationships into a self-organized low-dimensional space, and
density-based clustering using DBSCAN, followed by quantitative evaluation.
When applied to a publicly available dataset, the framework differentiated between
Parkinsonian and healthy gait patterns, achieving an NMI of 0.449 and an SCR of 6.754,
indicating a well-structured clustering organization. For benchmarking purposes, standard
classification metrics were also calculated, yielding an accuracy of 90%, a sensitivity of 70%,
and a specificity of 96.7%. Misclassifications were predominantly observed in individuals
with mild motor symptoms, as reflected in lower UPDRS-II scores, suggesting that the
method is sensitive to the gradation of gait alterations rather than to strict binary diagnostic
categories. These results indicate that ICR trajectories capture biomechanical variability
associated with PD, particularly in more pronounced cases, while also highlighting the
challenges inherent in detecting subtle early-stage deviations.
Beyond the specific application to PD, this work establishes a methodological founda-
tion for investigating gait patterns through unsupervised analysis of compact kinematic
descriptors. By combining interpretability, scalability, and modest acquisition requirements
compatible with single-camera setups, the ICR-LLS framework may support future research
aimed at objective gait characterization across neurological and musculoskeletal conditions.
https://doi.org/10.3390/app16083976

--- PAGE 22 ---
Appl. Sci. 2026, 16, 3976 22 of 24
Nevertheless, further validation in larger, clinically heterogeneous cohorts is necessary
before considering translational or clinical implementation.

project administration, L.M.A. and M.S.; funding acquisition, L.M.A. All authors have read and
agreed to the published version of the manuscript.

data set of walking full-body kinematics and kinetics in individuals with Parkinson’s disease at
10.3389/fnins.2023.992585, and A full-body motion capture gait dataset of 138 able-bodied adults
across the life span and 50 stroke survivors that can be found: https://www.nature.com/articles/s4
1597-023-02767-y, accessed on 16 April 2026, reference number [28,29].
